https://www.euronews.com/2026/11/26/tui-.text: TUI Group is regarded as the world's largest integrated tourism group. The firm includes around 460 hotels, 19 cruise ships, five airlines with 125 aircraft and around 1,200 travel agencies with a total of 67,000 employees.In 2025 the tourism group, headquartered in Hanover, generated revenue of €24.2 billion and an operating profit before interest and taxes of €1.46 billion.On 9 December the travel group will present its annual figures for 2026.Euronews spoke to Sebastian Ebel at an economic and innovation summit on the cruise ship "Mein Schiff Flow" in the northern-German city of Kiel.Euronews: In your view, what should the EU do to stimulate the economy and strengthen competitiveness?Sebastian Ebel: Bureaucracy is not only the EU's responsibility, national governments are responsible for it as well. I always use Denmark as an example: just as much a member of the EU as Germany, but with a far lower density of regulation. That is perhaps the first point, that we should organise these things that we can regulate ourselves, ourselves and differently and better. Of course in my view the EU apparatus, and I am a convinced European, it is the best peace model we have ever had, needs to be reformed. That includes streamlining it, cutting back regulation and focusing on guard rails.Euronews: Businesses also complain about labour shortages. Demographic trends in Europe will make the problem even worse. How do you assess this for your sector and for your company?Sebastian Ebel: I think we face a demographic factor that is challenging. When an age pyramid turns upside down, far fewer people have to support far more older people. That means that, mathematically, we have to work longer, at least those who want to and are able to. And it also means that we need immigration, specifically talented people who can solve the problems we have here. By the way, that is nothing new. I remember the waves in Braunschweig and Wolfsburg of Italians who came to work for VW. I remember people from the Philippines who came here for medical services. The point is that we bring the right people here who can strongly support us in this demographic transition so that it does not backfire on us.Euronews: Which political and economic framework conditions, the big levers, do we need in Germany and Europe to boost the economy?Sebastian Ebel: Cutting bureaucracy is the main point for me. If you work here every day as an entrepreneur, you know what you are talking about. Many people are not aware of the obstacles that exist. This also includes taxonomies, that is, a tax system that is simple, it is not always about cuts, but about it being manageable and understandable. Bureaucracy is a key issue.Euronews: The economy needs affordable energy and stable energy. It has to be available all the time. But can we really supply an industrial country with sustainable energy?Sebastian Ebel: Of course. Why not? It is the energy that is produced in the most sustainable and most cost effective way, and increasingly it can be produced even better in the future. Today we are failing because we do not have smart grids, so that we can deal with different situations, a lot of energy when it is stormy outside, little energy when it is dark and there is no wind, and cannot get this to the customer.Euronews: What about storage capacity? That is needed as well.Sebastian Ebel: There are three things. First, using the energy we have in such a way that when there is a lot of energy it is cheap and when there is little it is expensive, so that self-regulation takes place. The second issue is expanding the grids. That will increasingly be important. And third, working in large interconnected systems.Euronews: The EU says nuclear energy is climate friendly and can certainly be used. Do you share that view?Sebastian Ebel: There are new generations of nuclear energy. However, the question is whether there is majority support for it among the population. I have serious doubts whether this is achievable here. In other countries it is, including for example Sweden. I believe this question is not really on the agenda at the moment. Who today would want to build and put into operation a new nuclear power plant in Brokdorf? I think renewable energy can largely cover demand here and at very, very low prices.Euronews: What is TUI's position on electric mobility? E-ships will never exist.Sebastian Ebel: We were one of the first groups to say that we would only have company cars that are electric. We decided that two or three years ago and today we are glad we did. We are electrifying our bus fleets, we operate around 1,000 buses with partners worldwide. And we are now slowly beginning to switch to electric buses. We have the topic of hotels, in other words moving away from fossil fuels towards electric energy or geothermal energy to generate power.Ships have a major advantage, as we have heard today: LNG-powered ships. They should not run on fracked LNG, but on biogas energy from slurry. We can also produce methanol for traditional e-methanol. The big issue remains air travel. Today it is the most demanding area when it comes to making it carbon neutral in the long or medium term.Euronews: In your opinion, which fuels currently offer the greatest potential, in other words sustainable fuels?Sebastian Ebel: For ships, I believe very strongly in e-LNG or biogas LNG. And as a second step, methanol. I think this shift in the way the economy sources energy over a defined short period is perfectly feasible and today there is no longer a contradiction between economics and ecology, they go hand in hand. There are, however, some sectors, such as aviation, where there are still real issues that require technological change. Although I was able to learn again today that perhaps we are not that far away from this. When I see that a country like Denmark is completely independent of fossil gas, and that ships here can be fuelled with Danish e-LNG, then this, produced from slurry from livestock farming, water, slurry, straw, is really a model that we could implement in Germany or other European countries in exactly the same way.Euronews: An important topic is digital sovereignty. Why do we need to become independent of the US players? We could work well with them.Sebastian Ebel: I think it is important for security reasons, but also for economic reasons. We have just seen again that Starlink was switched off or reduced for Ukraine. I do not want us in Germany to be dependent on the decision of a single man in America as to whether we get a product or not. I believe it is our responsibility, not only for defence but also for economic enterprises. We must not be vulnerable to blackmail. That is one issue. The other is an economic issue. When I look at the margins of our German car industry and the tourism sector in Germany compared with software companies, the balance of power has been suspended. There high margins, here low margins. And I see that where companies have their own software again, negotiations also go better.Euronews: How are you using AI, artificial intelligence, at TUI?Sebastian Ebel: We started with flagship projects. We began with optimising route planning and deployment planning. We have used it very extensively in sales to find new distribution channels. And now, through AI factories, as we call them, we are producing software applications, ideally like in a factory(Editor's note: AI stands for Artificial Intelligence, German "Künstliche Intelligenz").Euronews: Tourism, a brief look back. How has 2026 been for TUI so far?Sebastian Ebel: 2026 was another difficult year. On top of all the economic developments, the war in the east and the challenges in the west, the war involving Iran was added. We had a one off effect because ships were held there and for two or three months we saw a very sharp slowdown in bookings, with long haul travel also heavily affected. Against this backdrop we have performed very, very well. We did not have to withdraw the guidance (Editor's note: the official forecast by the management for future business development) that we issued three months ago. The resilience that we as TUI have shown is something not everyone would have credited us with.Euronews: What are the trend destinations of the future, if we look a bit ahead?Sebastian Ebel: Cruises will remain strong. I would say everything related to experiences will grow even more. Whether it is a theme park, the best diving spot or a Dine&Wine course. Market segmentation will become more intense. And then, perhaps as the overarching effect, many people have a fixed budget, especially in economically challenging times. Offering something for this budget, for a single mother or father with one child or for grandparents with their grandchildren, that is one of our main tasks.Euronews: Overtourism is always an issue. Cruise ships are viewed very critically as well. But what positive effects does tourism have?Sebastian Ebel: Tourism is seen as extremely positive in the destinations. What we often do here is focus on what happens at two demonstrations in Mallorca. Worldwide, tourism is seen very, very positively. And there are regions, also in Germany by the way, that suffer from overtourism. In such cases it is up to governments to say what kind of tourism they want. Because if the people on the ground are not happy, then the customers are not either.And the point is that we are told what kind of tourism is wanted. The main point of criticism is often transport and, in particular, housing. Housing is the overriding issue when people still live at home at 25 because they can no longer afford a flat, or houses are always bought by foreigners at higher prices. And there I would recommend that those responsible introduce regulation so that people get the right kind of tourism and in the right quantity.Euronews: If you could make three or four decisions, if you were the President of the Commission or the German Chancellor, what are the three or four most important decisions where you would say: we have to take these now, otherwise time will run out on us?Sebastian Ebel: Massive cutting of bureaucracy. Bringing energy prices down to an acceptable level, launching an education offensive for talent, in other words upgrading schools and universities, and making sure that investment pays off again.Euronews: Thank you very much for the interview.Sebastian Ebel: My pleasure.
